(1) ribbon half-cycles of the Grand Cycles of the Upper Cambrian are composed of ribbon rock and interlaminated shale and (2) the shale content of ribbon half-cycles is a function of (a) the rate of terrigenous-sed-iment influx, (b) the rate of ribbon rock accumulation, and (c) the relative sea level of the platform.
Grand cycles are composed of ribbon half cycles and oolitic cycles.

the Grand Cycles of the Upper Cambrian in western Newfoundland were controlled by (1) changes of sea level, which were the primary control on the overall pattern, (2) terrigenous-sediments influx, which was the primary control on shale deposition, and (3), carbonate productivity, which was the principal control on the carbonate lithofacies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

(1) sea-level changes were the principal control on the distribution and geometry of Grand Cycles; (2) terrigenous-sedimentary input onto the platform had a profound effect on the carbonate productivity of the platform and, thus, on the distribution and thickness of ribbon and oolitic lithofacies; and (3) the terrigenous-sediments were derived from a hinterland that was undergoing tectonic instability.

sea level is the primary control on the distribution of carbonate and terrigenous lithofacies in the Upper Cambrian of western Newfoundland, but the influence of sea level on carbonate productivity and the influx of terrigenous fines is not always straightforward.

the Upper Cambrian strata in western Newfoundland were deposited on a shallow-marine, mixed siliciclastic-carbonate platform that experienced a series of large-amplitude, third-order sea-level cycles.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the distribution of terrigenous clastic sediment is controlled by the interaction between sea level and terrigenous sediment flux (the "sediment supply"), and that the distribution of carbonate lithofacies is controlled by the interplay between sea-level change and carbonate productivity (the "sedimentary factory").

sea level and carbonate productivity, as reflected in the distribution of oolitic facies, exerted a first-order control over the distribution of terrigenous clay on the paleoshelf of western Newfoundland.

the stratigraphic distribution of terrigenous clay in the Upper Cambrian of western Newfoundland is controlled by (1) third-order sea level and (2) the relative rates of carbonate production versus terrigenous sedimentation.
